lead: Magnetostrictive sensors use a magnetic material that changes length in a magnetic field, and changes its magnetization when stressed. The same coupling runs both ways. A coil can drive the material to make sound or strain; a force can change the material to make a coil voltage. These sensors measure force, torque and position and generate ultrasound. They are rugged and can take high force, so they appear in machine shafts, sonar, cleaning baths and delay lines.
prereq: You need Unit 2's magneto-resistive sensors for the magnetic-field background.

blocks.text: A magnetostrictive material changes shape when a magnetic field passes through it. This is the Joule effect. The fractional change in length is λ = ΔL / L, where ΔL is the change in length in metres and L is the original length in metres. λ is dimensionless. Engineers often quote it in ppm (parts per million): 1 ppm = 10⁻⁶. A positive λ means the rod expands; a negative λ means it contracts.

blocks.where: λ is the magnetostriction as a dimensionless fraction; multiply by 10⁶ to express it in ppm. ΔL and L are in the same unit.

blocks.text: The inverse is the Villari effect: stress applied to the material changes its magnetization. A pickup coil around the rod sees this as a voltage. The Wiedemann effect is a twist: a longitudinal field and a circumferential field together make the rod twist. These three effects give force, torque and delay-line sensors.

The curve of λ against field is not a straight line. Without a bias field it is nonlinear with hysteresis: it starts with near-zero slope at H = 0, rises steeply at intermediate field and then saturates. The same field can give different strains on the rising and falling path. A permanent magnet or a DC current in a coil sets a bias field. The sensor then works on a steeper, straighter part of the curve. Bias also decides the sign of the output for small changes.

Nickel gives small negative magnetostriction and is cheap and stable. Metglas, an amorphous alloy, has low loss and fast response with modest strain. Terfenol-D, a rare-earth iron alloy, gives large strain up to about 1000 to 2000 ppm and high force, but it is costly and brittle.

A magneto-elastic torque sensor uses a shaft with a magnetostrictive band or ring. Two coils sit near the shaft. Torque puts the band under shear stress. The Villari effect changes the magnetic permeability along one diagonal and reduces it along the other. The coils see a change in inductance or induced voltage. The output is proportional to torque over a limited range. Such sensors are non-contact and need no slip rings on a rotating shaft.

A magnetostrictive delay line sends a current pulse through a wire or ribbon. The pulse makes a local strain and a magnetic wave. A pickup coil at a known distance detects the wave. The delay is set by length and by the speed of the magneto-elastic wave. A force on the line changes the speed or the loss, so the delay or amplitude carries the measurement. These lines also make delay elements in older memories and filters.

A magnetostrictive ultrasonic transducer uses a coil around a nickel or Terfenol-D rod. An AC current at the resonant frequency makes the rod expand and contract and launch sound. At the receiving end, sound strains the rod and the coil gives a voltage. This is the magnetic cousin of the piezoelectric transducer in Section 4.1. Sonar, welding, cleaning and level sensing use it where ruggedness matters.

The strengths are high force capacity, a solid metal body, tolerance of high temperature, and simple coils with no sliding contacts. The weaknesses are hysteresis, nonlinearity, eddy-current loss at high frequency, and a need for stable bias.

Bias is the first design choice. A small permanent magnet in the rod or a DC current in a bias coil moves the operating point away from the flat, quadratic zero-field region, where the slope dλ/dH is nearly zero, to the steepest, most linear part of the λ-H curve. The AC drive or the stress then rides on a steady field. The output becomes larger and more linear, but the bias itself must be stable; a drift in bias looks like a drift in force.

The second choice is mechanical prestress. A compressed rod can push and pull around a mean stress. Prestress also reduces the effect of temperature and makes the strain more repeatable. The rod and the coils are mounted in a rigid frame. The frame must take the reaction force without bending; otherwise the sensor reads its own mounting.

Signal conditioning is simple: an AC bridge or a tuned coil for the drive, a small induced voltage from the pickup, then a filter and a demodulator. The output is a DC voltage or a digital delay. Hysteresis, eddy currents and temperature are the main errors. Nickel is cheap and stable; Metglas gives fast response; Terfenol-D gives large strain and high force but is costly and brittle. Use the sensor when you need high force and a tough body, not when you need micrometre accuracy.

figure.caption: A drive coil sets a magnetic field in the rod and produces strain; a force input changes the rod magnetization, which the pickup coil turns into voltage.

spec.aria: Two paths: a drive coil strains a magnetostrictive rod, and an input force changes the rod magnetization to give a pickup-coil voltage.

examples.question: A Terfenol-D rod is 50 mm long. At a bias field its magnetostriction is 1200 ppm. Find the change in length in mm and in μm.
steps: Convert the strain to a dimensionless fraction: λ = 1200 ppm = 1200 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.200 × 10⁻³.
Write the original length in mm: L = 50 mm.
Convert to micrometres: 0.060 mm × 1000 μm/mm = 60 μm.
examples.answer: The rod changes length by 0.060 mm, which is 60 μm.
examples.check:
L_mm = 50.0
lam_ppm = 1200.0
lam = lam_ppm * 1e-6
delta_mm = lam * L_mm
delta_um = delta_mm * 1000.0
print(delta_mm)
print(delta_um)

traps: Do not use λ = ΔL/L with L in mm and ΔL in μm; convert both to the same unit first.
Magnetostriction is not linear without bias. A single sensitivity number is valid only near the chosen bias field.
The Villari effect is the inverse of Joule magnetostriction; the Wiedemann effect is twist, not simple expansion.
A magnetostrictive transducer is not a Hall sensor. Hall sensors read field with a semiconductor; magnetostrictive sensors change length or magnetization.
Hysteresis means the same stress can give different output on loading and unloading; do not calibrate one direction only.

quiz.q: Define Joule magnetostriction and give its formula.
quiz.a: Joule magnetostriction is the change in length of a magnetic material when a magnetic field is applied. λ = ΔL/L, where ΔL is the change in length and L is the original length.

quiz.q: Why is a bias field used in a magnetostrictive sensor?
quiz.a: Bias moves the operating point from the flat zero-field region, where the curve is quadratic and the sensitivity is near zero, to the steep part of the λ-H curve. It gives a larger and more linear output for small changes and sets the sign of the response. The bias must be stable, or the output drifts.

quiz.q: A nickel rod has λ = -40 ppm and L = 80 mm. Find ΔL in μm.
quiz.a: λ = -40 ppm = -40 × 10⁻⁶. ΔL = λL = -40 × 10⁻⁶ × 80 mm = -0.0032 mm. In μm: -0.0032 × 1000 = -3.2 μm. The rod contracts by 3.2 μm.

quiz.q: A magneto-elastic torque sensor gives different output when torque rises and falls. Give two causes and one fix.
quiz.a: Causes are magnetic hysteresis in the magnetostrictive band and mechanical hysteresis or backlash in the shaft mounting. Temperature drift in the bias does not cause direction dependence; it appears as an offset or span error. Fix by setting a stable bias, calibrating both loading directions, and using a rigid mounting with temperature compensation.
The Villari effect is the change in magnetization of a magnetic material when it is stressed. A pickup coil can convert this change into a voltage.

quiz.q: A magnetostrictive delay line is 0.20 m long and the magneto-elastic wave speed is 5000 m/s. Find the delay.
Why does a magnetostrictive ultrasonic transducer suit a high-force environment better than a piezoelectric ceramic?
quiz.a: The magnetostrictive rod is a solid metal body and can take high compressive force and high temperature; it can be clamped in a rigid frame. A piezoelectric ceramic is brittle and needs careful mounting. Magnetostrictive transducers are larger and less efficient, so use them for rugged low-frequency sonar or high-force applications, not small precision probes.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses magneto-elastic torque sensors in electric power steering and drive shafts, and magnetostrictive position sensors in hydraulic cylinders. Terfenol-D appears in high-power sonar and precision actuators. Newer work searches for rare-earth-free magnetostrictive alloys and thin-film versions for MEMS. Search for 'magneto-elastic torque sensor', 'Terfenol-D magnetostriction' and 'magnetostrictive delay line'.
